common_name: Nana Variegata Weigela (Compact Cream-Edged Variegated Weigela)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in average, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; the cream variegation holds best with a few hours of direct sun each day.

directions: A compact, dwarf sport of the species with narrow green leaves broadly edged in cream, holding its variegation through the growing season even where full-sized variegated weigela selections tend to fade. Clusters of rosy-pink, funnel-shaped flowers open against the pale foliage in a late-spring flush, giving a softer, more pastel effect than the species type. Its small mature size suits foundation plantings, mixed borders, and container culture where larger weigela cultivars would quickly outgrow the space. Prune lightly right after flowering, since blooms form on the previous year's wood, and remove any solid-green reverted shoots promptly as they grow more vigorously than the variegated wood.

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in average, well-drained soil in full sun; established plants tolerate heat and a range of garden soils without complaint.

directions: One of the oldest named weigela selections still grown, raised by the Belgian nursery firm of Louis Van Houtte in the mid-19th century and now uncommon in the nursery trade compared to modern cultivars. It makes a large, rounded shrub with carmine-red buds that open to funnel-shaped flowers aging to a deeper red-purple, creating a two-toned effect across the bush in a heavy late-spring flush. Its larger ultimate size suits a background position in a mixed shrub border or informal hedge rather than a tight foundation planting. Prune immediately after flowering to shape and renew the plant, since flower buds form on the previous season's wood.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (International Dendrology Society)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in average, well-drained soil; the cream-edged variegation makes this selection more tolerant of partial shade than plain-leaved deutzia types.

directions: A compact Proven Winners selection of slender deutzia grown chiefly for its dramatic cream-margined foliage, which brightens shaded corners and mixed borders even outside of bloom time. Frothy clusters of small white, star-shaped flowers open along the arching stems in late spring above the variegated leaves, and the foliage often takes on added color in fall. Its tidy, mounded habit suits foundation plantings, border edges, and container culture. Like other deutzia it flowers on the previous year's wood, so prune lightly right after bloom to maintain shape without sacrificing next year's display.

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade; tolerates both sunnier and shadier placements better than many other deutzia.

directions: Bred at the U.S. National Arboretum from a cross of Deutzia gracilis 'Nikko' with Deutzia x rosea 'Carminea' to combine Nikko's low, mounded habit with pink flower color. Bright pink buds open in a profuse spring flush to softer pink, mildly fragrant flowers along low, arching branches above fine-textured, willow-like foliage. Its low, spreading habit suits mass planting, border fronts, and slopes where a compact pink-flowered deutzia is wanted. Prune lightly right after flowering, since like other deutzia it blooms on the previous year's wood.

common_name: Really Pink Abelia (Historic Clear-Pink Flowered Abelia)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; now rare in commercial production compared to more widely marketed modern abelia cultivars.

directions: An older selection raised before the 1980s, resembling the popular hybrid 'Edward Goucher' in habit and evergreen-to-semi-evergreen foliage but distinguished by clearer, more saturated pink flowers rather than the lavender-pink tone typical of most abelia hybrids. Small, tubular, nectar-rich flowers open over a long season from late spring into fall and draw bees and butterflies steadily. Its dense, arching, multi-stemmed habit fits a mixed shrub border or informal hedge. Established plants tolerate heat and humidity well and need only an occasional shaping prune after the main flush to maintain a tidy form.

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in average, well-drained soil; the silvery-white leaf margins show best with a few hours of direct sun daily and take on added pink tones in cool weather.

directions: A compact, semi-evergreen selection grown primarily for its silvery-white and green variegated foliage, which emerges pink-tinged in spring and again colors up in autumn and winter cold. Fragrant, white to pale pink tubular flowers open from mid-spring into fall above the variegated leaves, drawing bees and butterflies without overshadowing the foliage display. Its low, dense habit suits foundation plantings, low hedging, and container culture. Established plants tolerate heat and short dry spells; remove any plain-green reverted shoots promptly since they grow faster than the variegated wood.

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; golden leaf margins develop most strongly with several hours of direct sun daily.

directions: A variegated selection of glossy abelia grown for its green leaves broadly margined in gold, giving a bright, two-toned effect through the growing season even before the small, fragrant, white-to-pale-pink tubular flowers open from late spring into fall. The long bloom season draws bees, butterflies, and hummingbirds steadily. Its arching, multi-stemmed habit fits a mixed shrub border, foundation planting, or informal hedge. Established plants tolerate heat, humidity, and short dry spells well; shape lightly after the main flowering flush and remove any solid-green reverted shoots promptly.
